1:
Who the evil man is nobody quite agrees. Gill collects the Jewish attributions — Saul, Doeg, or Esau, by which the last writer means Rome and the Christians, a reading Gill would allow only if confined to the Papists — then generalises to a body of evil men. Clarke names Saul, and reports that the Syriac dates the psalm to the moment when Saul tried to transfix David with his spear. Calvin refuses the majority: he cannot restrict the psalm to Doeg, as the great body of interpreters do, since the context shows it speaks of Saul and of the counsellors who never ceased inflaming an already incensed king. Henry takes Saul for the ring-leader too, noting that the Chaldee names both Doeg and Ahithophel though a great distance of time lay between them. Delitzsch goes elsewhere, explaining the psalm from Absalom's rebellion, to which the Benjamite Sheba's attached itself as an outbreak of Ephraimitish jealousy. Ellicott and Spurgeon both refuse the singular. It must not lead us, says Ellicott, to think this personal feeling against one enemy, since it is immediately changed to the plural; and Spurgeon says David pleads against the species rather than the individual, so that the line reads like a clause of the Lord's prayer.

Two readers defend the psalm's temper. Calvin insists David is not multiplying terms of reproach as men do in personal disputes, but conciliating God's favour by proving his innocence. Delitzsch grants the roughness — the psalm is more bold than beautiful in form — and observes that its language becomes fearfully obscure just where it is directed against the enemies.

Ellicott reports that others render they dwell with wars, but prefers a root meaning to incite: they are continually stirring up wars, Israel being at peace while others try to involve her in trouble.

The serpent draws out natural history. Gill reports a Jewish claim that the serpent sharpens its tongue before it bites, and the ancient observation that its tip is as fine as a hair; another refers the figure to the serpent's cunning, particularly the one that spoke to Eve. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew rendered adders occurs only here and has been explained as a compound meaning that which rolls itself up and lies in ambush, and adds a naturalist's report of the vipers common in Syria. Henry keeps the moral: poison in the lips is a certain sign of poison in the heart. Wesley reduces it to words as sharp as a serpent's sting.

The snares are the machinery of persecution. Gill takes the proud for the Ziphites and the cords for the fowler's. Clarke says David was hunted as a dangerous wild beast, to be sacrificed before the people as an enemy to the state. Ellicott calls the net a favourite image whose frequency indicates the dangers Israel ran from the leaning of many to foreign influences. Henry makes the sharpest observation: great persecutors have often been great politicians, which has made them the more formidable — but the Lord preserves the simple without those arts.

The turn to prayer is marked by all. Spurgeon dwells on the boldness of the confession: that had need be a full assurance which a man dares lay before the heart-searching Lord; and often the less we say to our foes and the more to our best Friend, the better. On the covered head Delitzsch takes the day of equipment for the day of crisis, when the battle is fought in full array, God protecting the anointed against the deadly blow. Ellicott renders it literally in the day of arms, when he was arming for the fight, though others take it for the day of battle itself. Augustine hears throughout the voice of the Church set among the wicked, and reads the deliverance as sought not from one man but from the whole class, and from their prince.
8:
The imprecations that close the psalm are the difficulty, and are met differently. Henry treats the eighth verse as a prayer of disappointment rather than destruction: let not providence favour their designs, but chain the wheels and stop them in their pursuits. He fastens on the reason — lest they exalt themselves: proud men, when they prosper, grow more impudent against God and more insolent against his people. He reports that where he prays, some read prophecy. Gill takes the verse of Doeg after the Targum, and observes that the desires of the wicked are under God's restraint. Clarke keeps to the Chaldee's Doeg.

Ellicott finds the text badly damaged: the versions insert a negative before the last word and take the phrase rendered wicked devices as a verb, no noun of that form being found elsewhere. He suggests that the verb lift up belongs to the following verse — they lift the head, these surrounding me — an arrangement that obliges him to suspect a clause has dropped out, as the rhythm confirms. At the tenth verse a further difficulty remains, since the subject of the next verb is singular; a slight change gives a plain sentence — let it bring upon themselves coals of fire, let it cast them into pits, so that they rise no more. One lexicographer renders the peculiar word for pits as whirlpools, combining water with fire as emblems of perils that cannot be escaped.

The coals are read as judgement in both worlds. Gill takes them as falling from heaven, alluding to Sodom, and covering both the judgments of this life and everlasting burnings. Clarke gives the Chaldee's paraphrase against Ahithophel — coals from heaven, the fire of hell, and miry pits from which they shall have no resurrection to eternal life — and draws the unexpected conclusion that this proves the Jews believed in a resurrection of the body. Wesley reduces the figure to divine vengeance. Spurgeon reads the ninth verse as retaliation with a certain relish: the Lord who had covered David's head amid the din of arms is asked to cover his enemies' heads quite otherwise, and they are represented as having but one head, since there is often a unanimity among evil spirits. When a man's lips vent curses they will, like chickens, come home to roost.

The man of tongue is identified from the versions. Gill applies it to one who sets his mouth against the heavens and whose tongue walks through the earth. Clarke finds much force in the Chaldee's man of detraction with the three-forked tongue, and explains it: such a man wounds three at once, the neighbour he slanders, the one who receives it, and himself who deals in it. Ellicott takes the phrase as literally a man of tongue and thinks it hardly possible to resist the suggestion that some particular person, noted for the violence of his speech, was meant; on the hunting of the violent man he compares Horace on the vengeance that seldom leaves the wretch it hounds.

The close is heard as a change of key. Delitzsch says the mood becomes cheerful again, the rage having spent itself, so that the psalm trips along merrily to the end; and he reads the promise as generalising into the triumph of the good cause what David elsewhere expects for himself alone. Spurgeon calls the psalm grandly positive, a protest against slander by a man who speaks only of things he does not doubt: the prosperous can maintain their own cause, but those who cannot help themselves find that God helps them. Clarke states it in a line: every man persecuted for righteousness has God for his help, and the persecutor has the same God for his enemy. Gill notes a double reading at the twelfth verse: the margin gives thou knowest, the text I know.
